Linear & Logistic Regression

Linear regression predicts a continuous target as a weighted sum of features, y = w·x + b. Logistic regression reuses that linear score but squashes it through the sigmoid σ(z)=1/(1+e^(-z)) to produce a probability for binary classification.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Linear regression draws the best straight line through a cloud of points. Logistic regression bends that line into an S so the output stays between 0 and 1, reading as a probability.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Linear regression is fit by minimizing mean squared error (MSE); it has a closed-form normal-equation solution or can use gradient descent. Logistic regression minimizes binary cross-entropy (log loss) and has no closed form, so it is trained iteratively by gradient descent.

Example: predicting house price from square footage is regression; predicting whether an email is spam (0/1) is logistic classification, where you threshold the probability at 0.5.

📝 KEY IDEA

Despite its name, logistic regression is a classification algorithm. It models the log-odds as a linear function of the inputs.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Do not use MSE to train logistic regression — MSE with a sigmoid is non-convex and slows learning. Use cross-entropy, which is convex in the weights.

📊 FIGURE — log-odds in, odds out
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Why 0.7 doubles the odds but not the probability

A coefficient of 0.7 multiplies the odds by e^0.7 = 2.0138 ≈ 2.01. What that does to the probability depends entirely on the starting point:

  • from p = 0.10 (odds 0.111) → odds 0.224 → p = 0.183, a jump of 8.3 points
  • from p = 0.50 (odds 1.000) → odds 2.014 → p = 0.668, a jump of 16.8 points
  • from p = 0.90 (odds 9.000) → odds 18.12 → p = 0.948, a jump of only 4.8 points

The odds ratio is constant at 2.01 in all three cases; the probability change is not. That is exactly why logistic coefficients are reported as odds ratios rather than as \"percentage point\" effects.

🎯 EXAM TIP
A logistic coefficient of 0.7 multiplies the odds of the positive class by e^0.7 ≈ 2.01. Coefficients are additive in log-odds and therefore multiplicative in odds — and the effect on the probability is not constant, since it depends on where you started.
"}, "AIM-ML/ch1/s2": {"body": "

Decision Trees, Random Forests & Gradient Boosting

A decision tree splits data with a sequence of yes/no questions, choosing splits that reduce impurity (Gini or entropy for classification, variance for regression). Single trees overfit, so we combine many.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

One decision tree is a single opinionated expert who can be wrong. A random forest asks hundreds of slightly different experts and votes. Boosting instead lines up experts so each one fixes the previous one's mistakes.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Random forests use bagging: train many deep trees on bootstrap samples with random feature subsets, then average or vote. This reduces variance. Gradient boosting builds shallow trees sequentially, each fit to the residual errors (negative gradient of the loss) of the current ensemble, reducing bias.

Example: XGBoost and LightGBM are gradient-boosted tree libraries that dominate tabular-data problems in 2026. A random forest with hundreds of trees rarely overfits badly because averaging cancels the individual trees' errors, whereas a boosting model can overfit if you add too many trees or use too high a learning rate, so early stopping on a validation set is standard practice.

📝 KEY IDEA

Bagging (forests) reduces variance by averaging independent trees; boosting reduces bias by correcting errors step by step.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Random forests train trees independently and in parallel; boosting is inherently sequential. Confusing the two — or thinking boosting averages independent trees — is a classic error.

"}, "AIM-ML/ch1/s3": {"body": "

Support Vector Machines

A support vector machine (SVM) finds the hyperplane that separates two classes with the largest margin — the widest gap to the nearest points. Those nearest points are the support vectors; they alone define the boundary.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Imagine drawing the widest possible street between two groups of houses. The SVM boundary runs down the middle of the street, and the houses touching the curb are the support vectors.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

A soft-margin SVM allows some misclassifications, controlled by the penalty C: large C punishes errors heavily (narrow margin, risk of overfit); small C allows more slack. The kernel trick (e.g. RBF, polynomial) computes inner products in a higher-dimensional space so a linear separator there becomes a nonlinear boundary in the original space — without ever computing the transformed coordinates.

Example: an RBF-kernel SVM can separate concentric-ring data that no straight line could split. In practice you tune both C and the kernel's gamma together, often by grid search with cross-validation, because gamma controls how far the influence of a single training point reaches while C controls the error penalty.

📝 KEY IDEA

Only the support vectors matter; moving or removing non-support points does not change the boundary.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

A large C is not 'more regularization'. Large C means less tolerance for errors and a tighter fit — it can overfit, not underfit.

"}, "AIM-ML/ch1/s4": {"body": "

Clustering & Dimensionality Reduction

These are unsupervised methods — no labels. K-means partitions points into k groups by iteratively assigning each point to the nearest centroid and recomputing centroids. PCA (principal component analysis) finds orthogonal directions of maximum variance to compress features.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

K-means is like sorting a pile of mixed marbles into k bowls by color, adjusting each bowl's average color until things settle. PCA is like photographing a 3-D object from the angle that reveals the most detail in a flat picture.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

K-means minimizes within-cluster sum of squares; you must pick k in advance (the elbow method or silhouette score helps). PCA projects data onto the top eigenvectors of the covariance matrix — the principal components — ordered by explained variance. t-SNE and UMAP are nonlinear techniques used mainly for 2-D visualization, not as general-purpose feature compressors.

Example: reducing 784-pixel MNIST digits to 2 PCA components lets you plot clusters of digits.

📝 KEY IDEA

PCA is linear and preserves global variance; t-SNE and UMAP emphasize local neighborhood structure for visualization.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

K-means assumes roughly spherical, equally sized clusters and is sensitive to initialization and k. It can converge to a poor local optimum — use k-means++ initialization and multiple restarts.

"}, "AIM-ML/ch1/s5": {"body": "

Model Evaluation & the Bias-Variance Tradeoff

Good evaluation separates a model that memorizes from one that generalizes. We hold out a test set and use cross-validation on the training data to tune hyperparameters.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Studying for an exam by memorizing the practice answers (overfitting) fails on new questions. Barely skimming the material (underfitting) fails everywhere. You want understanding that transfers — low error on questions you have never seen.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Bias is error from oversimplified assumptions (underfitting); variance is error from over-sensitivity to the training data (overfitting). Total error is approximately bias squared plus variance plus irreducible noise. For imbalanced classification, accuracy misleads — use precision, recall, F1, and ROC-AUC. Precision = TP/(TP+FP); recall = TP/(TP+FN).

Example: a fraud detector that predicts 'not fraud' for everyone can be 99% accurate yet have zero recall — useless. The F1 score, the harmonic mean of precision and recall, summarizes both in one number, while the ROC-AUC measures ranking quality across all thresholds and is insensitive to the chosen cutoff.

📝 KEY IDEA

High bias means underfit (train and test error both high). High variance means overfit (low train error, high test error).

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Never tune hyperparameters on the test set. Doing so leaks information and inflates your reported performance; use a validation split or cross-validation instead.

"}, "AIM-ML/ch2/s1": {"body": "

Neural Networks: Perceptrons, Activations & Loss Functions

A perceptron computes a weighted sum plus bias and applies an activation. Stacking many such units into layers gives a multilayer perceptron (MLP) that can approximate complex functions.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Each neuron is a tiny voter: it weighs its inputs, adds them up, and decides how loudly to fire. Layers of these voters combine simple opinions into sophisticated decisions.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Without a nonlinear activation, stacked linear layers collapse into a single linear map. ReLU (max(0,x)) is the default hidden activation — cheap and avoids vanishing gradients for positive inputs. Softmax turns a vector of logits into a probability distribution for multi-class output. Loss: MSE for regression; cross-entropy for classification.

import torch.nn as nn\nnet = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(4,16), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(16,3))

This small network maps a 4-feature input to 3 class logits. The universal approximation theorem tells us that even a single sufficiently wide hidden layer with a nonlinear activation can approximate any continuous function, but in practice deeper networks learn richer features more efficiently than one enormous layer.

📝 KEY IDEA

Use ReLU (or variants like GELU) in hidden layers; use softmax plus cross-entropy at the output for multi-class problems.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Applying softmax yourself and then using nn.CrossEntropyLoss double-counts the softmax — CrossEntropyLoss expects raw logits and applies log-softmax internally.

📊 FIGURE — what the activation does
🎯 EXAM TIP
ReLU on pre-activations [−2, 0, 3] gives [0, 0, 3] — it is max(0, x) applied to each entry on its own, not across the vector. Contrast softmax, which does couple the entries because it divides by their sum. The derivative being exactly 1 for positive inputs is what prevents the vanishing-gradient problem that sigmoid has.
"}, "AIM-ML/ch2/s2": {"body": "

Backpropagation & Training

Backpropagation computes the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight by applying the chain rule backward through the network. An optimizer then nudges the weights to reduce the loss.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Backprop is like tracing blame backwards through a chain of coworkers: the final error is distributed to each earlier step in proportion to how much it contributed, so everyone knows how to adjust.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Training loops through: forward pass, compute loss, loss.backward() (backprop fills .grad), optimizer.step() (update weights), then optimizer.zero_grad(). The learning rate scales each step. SGD updates from mini-batches; Adam adapts per-parameter step sizes using running moment estimates.

optimizer.zero_grad()\nloss = criterion(model(x), y)\nloss.backward()\noptimizer.step()

Those four lines are the heart of nearly every PyTorch training loop, repeated over mini-batches for many epochs. Additional tricks such as learning-rate schedules that decay the step over time, momentum that smooths noisy gradients, and gradient clipping that caps exploding gradients all build on this same skeleton to make training faster and more stable.

📝 KEY IDEA

Always call optimizer.zero_grad() before backward — PyTorch accumulates gradients by default, so stale grads would otherwise pile up.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

A learning rate that is too high makes loss diverge (NaN); too low makes training crawl. It is the single most important hyperparameter to tune.

"}, "AIM-ML/ch2/s3": {"body": "

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs)

CNNs excel at images. A convolution slides small learnable filters (kernels) across the input, detecting local patterns like edges, then textures, then object parts as layers deepen.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A convolution filter is like a small stencil you slide over a photo, lighting up wherever it finds its pattern — an edge, a corner. Stack stencils and you recognize eyes, then faces.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Key properties: parameter sharing (the same kernel is reused across all positions, so far fewer weights than a dense layer) and translation equivariance (a feature is detected wherever it appears). Pooling (e.g. max pooling) downsamples, adding some translation invariance and shrinking spatial size. Deeper layers grow the receptive field.

conv = nn.Conv2d(in_channels=3, out_channels=16, kernel_size=3, padding=1)

This layer takes a 3-channel (RGB) image and produces 16 feature maps using 3x3 kernels. A typical CNN stacks several such convolution-plus-pooling blocks to extract increasingly abstract features, then flattens the result into fully connected layers that output class scores. Modern image models like ResNet also add skip connections so gradients flow cleanly through very deep stacks.

📝 KEY IDEA

Convolutional layers share weights across space, drastically cutting parameters versus fully connected layers and building in a locality prior.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Forgetting padding shrinks feature maps at every layer; use padding to preserve spatial dimensions when you intend a 'same' convolution.

"}, "AIM-ML/ch2/s4": {"body": "

RNNs & LSTMs

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) process sequences one step at a time, carrying a hidden state that summarizes the past. LSTMs add gates so they can remember information over long spans.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

An RNN reads a sentence like a person reading left to right, keeping a running mental summary. A plain RNN forgets the start of a long paragraph; an LSTM has a notepad (the cell state) it can deliberately write to and erase.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Plain RNNs suffer vanishing and exploding gradients over long sequences, so they struggle with long-range dependencies. LSTMs introduce a cell state and three gates — forget, input, and output — that regulate what information is kept, added, or exposed. GRUs are a lighter variant with two gates. RNNs are inherently sequential, limiting parallelism.

rnn = nn.LSTM(input_size=100, hidden_size=256, batch_first=True)

Here each time step ingests a 100-dimensional vector and the LSTM maintains a 256-dimensional hidden state. Bidirectional variants read the sequence both forward and backward to use future context, and stacking multiple LSTM layers deepens the model. For years these networks powered machine translation and speech recognition before attention-based models took over.

📝 KEY IDEA

The LSTM cell state acts as a gradient highway, letting information and gradients flow across many time steps.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Because they process tokens one at a time, RNNs cannot parallelize across the sequence during training — a key reason Transformers replaced them for large-scale NLP.

"}, "AIM-ML/ch2/s5": {"body": "

Transformers

Transformers replaced recurrence with self-attention, letting every token directly attend to every other token in parallel. They are the backbone of modern large language models in 2026.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

Instead of reading a sentence strictly left to right, attention lets each word look at the whole sentence at once and decide which other words matter most to its meaning — like a reader who can glance anywhere on the page instantly.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Self-attention builds Query, Key, and Value vectors per token. Attention weights = softmax(QK^T/√d_k), then multiplied by V. Multi-head attention runs several attentions in parallel. Because attention is order-agnostic, positional encodings inject sequence order. Blocks also include feed-forward layers, residual connections, and layer normalization.

attn = nn.MultiheadAttention(embed_dim=512, num_heads=8, batch_first=True)

This module splits a 512-dimensional embedding across 8 heads of 64 dimensions each. A subtlety is that naive attention costs grow quadratically with sequence length, so 2026-era long-context models rely on optimized kernels like FlashAttention and various sparse or linear-attention schemes to scale to very long inputs efficiently.

📝 KEY IDEA

Self-attention is fully parallel across positions, which is why Transformers train far faster on modern hardware than RNNs.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Attention alone has no notion of order — remove positional encodings and 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' look identical to the model.

📊 FIGURE — which pair makes the weights
🎯 EXAM TIP
Self-attention computes its weights from queries and keys — softmax(QKᵀ/√d_k) — and only then applies them to the values. The division by √d_k keeps the dot products from growing with dimension and pushing softmax into a saturated, near-one-hot regime.
"}, "AIM-ML/ch2/s6": {"body": "

PyTorch Essentials

PyTorch centers on the tensor — an n-dimensional array with GPU support and automatic differentiation. Models subclass nn.Module; training uses autograd plus an optimizer.

💡 IN PLAIN ENGLISH

A tensor is like a NumPy array that also keeps a memory of every operation done to it, so it can retrace its steps to compute gradients automatically.

⚙️ HOW IT WORKS

Set requires_grad=True (parameters do this automatically) and autograd builds a dynamic graph on the forward pass. A custom model defines __init__ (layers) and forward (computation). Move tensors and models to GPU with .to('cuda'). Switch modes with model.train() and model.eval(), and wrap inference in torch.no_grad() to skip graph building.

class Net(nn.Module):\n    def __init__(self):\n        super().__init__()\n        self.fc = nn.Linear(10, 2)\n    def forward(self, x):\n        return self.fc(x)

Calling model(x) runs the forward pass; list(model.parameters()) exposes the learnable tensors you hand to an optimizer such as torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3). Save and reload weights with torch.save(model.state_dict(), path) and model.load_state_dict(...), which stores only the parameters rather than the whole Python object.

📝 KEY IDEA

Never call forward manually — invoke the model as model(x), which triggers hooks and calls forward for you.

⚠️ COMMON TRAP

Forgetting model.eval() at inference leaves dropout and batchnorm in training mode, silently corrupting predictions.

💡 KEY RESULTS\n

BatchNorm normalizes each feature over the batch (μ,σ² per channel) then scales by γ,β: 2·C learnable params. LayerNorm normalizes over features per sample — batch-independent, used in Transformers. Gradient magnitude scales like ∏‖Wₗ‖: <1 vanishes, >1 explodes (0.9⁵⁰≈0.005, 1.1⁵⁰≈117). BN couples samples in a batch (breaks with batch size 1); LN does not. A 1×1 conv still has Cin·Cout params but K=1. FLOPs are usually reported as 2×MACs (multiply+add).

Regularization & Kernels

\n

Ridge minimizes ||y-Xw||^2 + lambda||w||^2 with solution w=(X^TX+lambda I)^{-1}X^Ty; increasing lambda shrinks coefficients smoothly along the regularization path. Lasso (L1) instead yields sparse, piecewise-linear paths (LARS).

\n

⚙️ FORMULAS

  • Ridge: w=(X^TX+lambda I)^{-1}X^Ty
  • Kernel: K(x,x')=<phi(x),phi(x')>; RKHS norm penalizes complexity.
  • Ensemble variance (corr rho): rho*sigma^2 + (1-rho)/B * sigma^2
  • F1 =2PR/(P+R); AUC = P(score+ > score-).
\n

💡 KEY RESULTS

  • Kernel trick: work in high-dim feature space via inner products only, never forming phi.
  • Gradient boosting = functional gradient descent: each tree fits the negative gradient of the loss (residuals for squared loss).
  • VC dimension of linear classifiers in R^d is d+1; generalization gap scales like sqrt(VC/n).
\n

📝 DERIVATION

For squared loss L=1/2(y-F)^2, the functional gradient w.r.t. prediction F is -(y-F), so boosting fits the residual. For logistic loss the pseudo-residual is y-p.

\n

⚠️ SUBTLETY

AUC is threshold-independent and insensitive to class balance, but a high AUC can still hide poor calibration and poor precision under heavy imbalance. Averaging correlated models cannot push variance below rho*sigma^2.

\n

EM for GMMs alternates E-step responsibilities gamma_k=pi_k N_k / sum pi_j N_j and M-step weighted MLE updates; it maximizes a lower bound (ELBO) and monotonically increases likelihood.

Optimization & Modern Architectures

\n

Adam keeps EMA moments m,v, bias-corrects them, and updates theta -= lr * m_hat/(sqrt(v_hat)+eps). AdamW decouples weight decay: it subtracts lr*wd*theta separately rather than folding decay into the gradient.

\n

⚙️ FORMULAS

  • Adam: m_hat=m/(1-b1^t), v_hat=v/(1-b2^t)
  • Attention: softmax(QK^T/sqrt(d_k))V
  • Inverted dropout scale: 1/(1-p)
  • KV cache bytes: 2*L*seq*d_model*bytes*batch
\n

💡 KEY RESULTS

  • Residual connections let gradients flow via an identity path, so dL/dx includes an unattenuated +1 term, mitigating vanishing gradients.
  • Dropout approximates an ensemble of exponentially many sub-networks.
  • Chinchilla scaling: compute-optimal training uses roughly 20 tokens per parameter.
\n

📝 DERIVATION

The 1/sqrt(d_k) factor keeps QK^T variance O(1): for unit-variance independent q,k, the dot product over d_k dims has variance d_k, so dividing by sqrt(d_k) prevents softmax saturation and tiny gradients.

\n

⚠️ SUBTLETY

BatchNorm normalizes across the batch (statistics depend on other samples; unstable for small batches/sequences), while LayerNorm normalizes across features per-sample (batch-independent), which is why transformers use LayerNorm. Mixed precision needs loss scaling to stop fp16 gradient underflow.

\n

Learning-rate schedules (linear warmup then cosine decay) stabilize early training; gradient clipping bounds the update norm to prevent exploding gradients in deep/recurrent stacks.

\n
THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its \"J-Method\"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
\n
